explanations.explanation: That's it. Naomi, Ruth's mother-in-law, asks, “…should I not seek a resting place for you, that it may be well with you?” (Ruth 3:1) Notice she's thinking about how things go for Ruth, not just herself. I've been tucked in a drawer, so a good resting place sounds like a WONDERFUL thing to me.

Close to Ruth's world, but not what Naomi says. Naomi, Ruth's mother-in-law, knows Ruth has been gleaning in Boaz's fields (Ruth 2:23). A field of her own never comes up in Ruth 3:1. What Naomi says she wants to seek is “…a resting place…”

Ruth is from Moab (Ruth 1:22), so I see why this one tempts you. But Naomi, Ruth's mother-in-law, never says a word about Moab in this verse. She says she wants to seek “…a resting place…” for Ruth, “…that it may be well with you?” Right now Ruth is living with Naomi, and Naomi's mind is on what comes next.

Yes, relative. Naomi says, “Now is not Boaz, with whose servant girls you have been working, a relative of ours?” (Ruth 3:2) So Boaz is more than the man whose servant girls Ruth has been working with. He's family. That detail is going to matter, friend.

A neighbor would be somebody who lives nearby, and that's not what Naomi says. She calls Boaz “…a relative of ours?” That's family, which is a much bigger deal than waving over the fence. Hold onto that word, because it's going to keep showing up.

Easy mix-up, since Naomi does mention servant girls in the same breath. But those are Boaz's servant girls, the ones Ruth has been working with. Boaz himself is called “…a relative of ours?” The servants are in the verse, but Boaz isn't one of them.

That's the spot. Naomi says, “In fact, tonight he is winnowing barley on the threshing floor.” (Ruth 3:2) Winnowing is how the grain gets separated from the chaff. Naomi knows where Boaz will be AND what he'll be doing, friend.

The city gate shows up later in Ruth, where Boaz goes up to it and sits down (Ruth 4:1), so it's a fair guess. But Naomi doesn't send Ruth there. She says Boaz is winnowing barley on the threshing floor. That's where the work is happening tonight.

explanations.answer: In the shelter by the field
explanations.explanation: A shelter by the field sounds cozy, but the text never mentions one. Naomi says Boaz is “…winnowing barley on the threshing floor.” (Ruth 3:2) Winnowing is the work, and the threshing floor is the place. No shelter anywhere in the verse.

This one is False, and here's what Naomi really says. She tells Ruth, “Therefore wash yourself, put on perfume, and wear your best clothes.” (Ruth 3:3) So Ruth is NOT heading down in her everyday work clothes. Naomi wants her cleaned up and in her best.

Right, it's False. Naomi tells Ruth, “Therefore wash yourself, put on perfume, and wear your best clothes.” (Ruth 3:3) That's the opposite of just showing up as she is. Wash, perfume, best clothes, in that order.

explanations.answer: After he finishes eating and drinking
explanations.explanation: Yes. Naomi says to go down to the threshing floor, “…but do not let the man know you are there until he has finished eating and drinking.” (Ruth 3:3) Timing is part of the plan. Ruth waits until Boaz is done with his meal.

explanations.answer: As soon as she gets there
explanations.explanation: Naomi says to go down to the threshing floor, “…but do not let the man know you are there until he has finished eating and drinking.” (Ruth 3:3) So Ruth can go down, but Boaz isn't supposed to know she's there yet. Letting him know the moment she arrives would skip the timing Naomi gave.

Naomi's marker isn't the sun, it's the meal: “…until he has finished eating and drinking.” (Ruth 3:3) That's the timing she gives. And Boaz is startled at midnight to find Ruth at his feet (Ruth 3:8), well before sunrise.
True. Naomi says that when Ruth lies down, “…he will explain to you what you should do.” (Ruth 3:4) Ruth isn't left to figure out the rest on her own. Boaz is the one who will tell her.

It's actually True. Naomi ends her instructions with, “…he will explain to you what you should do.” (Ruth 3:4) So Boaz is the one who will tell Ruth what comes next. Naomi hands Ruth the first steps, then the next part is Boaz's.

explanations.answer: I will do everything you say
explanations.explanation: That's Ruth. “I will do everything you say…” she answers. (Ruth 3:5) No stalling, no side questions. Compare that to me with a to-do list. I'd negotiate with MYSELF first.

explanations.answer: Let me think it over first
explanations.explanation: Plenty of us would say that, friend, myself included. But Ruth doesn't. She answers, “I will do everything you say…” (Ruth 3:5) And then verse 6 says she did everything her mother-in-law had instructed her to do.

Ruth doesn't ask Naomi to come along. She says, “I will do everything you say…” (Ruth 3:5) Then the text has her going down to the threshing floor and doing what Naomi told her. Nothing here says Naomi goes too.
This one is False. Ruth does the opposite of marching in. The text says, “Then Ruth went in secretly, uncovered his feet, and lay down.” (Ruth 3:7) No announcement, no grand entrance.
Right, False. Verse 7 says, “Then Ruth went in secretly, uncovered his feet, and lay down.” That's quiet, friend. If I tried sneaking in, my gold base would clunk and wake the whole bakery.

explanations.answer: Spread the corner of his garment over her
explanations.explanation: That's her request. Ruth, the Moabite who has been gleaning in his fields (Ruth 2:2, 3), says, “Spread the corner of your garment over me…” (Ruth 3:9) She tells Boaz who she is first, then she asks. Ruth knows what she's asking for.

explanations.answer: Walk her home to Naomi at first light
explanations.explanation: Nice thought, but Ruth doesn't ask for that. After telling Boaz who she is, she says, “Spread the corner of your garment over me…” (Ruth 3:9) Later, the text says Ruth gets up before anyone else could recognize her, and she returns to Naomi (Ruth 3:14, 16). The walk home isn't part of her request.

explanations.answer: Speak to the elders of the town for her
explanations.explanation: Elders aren't part of what she asks here. Ruth says, “Spread the corner of your garment over me…” (Ruth 3:9) That's her request, plain and direct. Boaz is the one who brings up a plan for the morning, and Ruth doesn't ask him to speak to anybody.
That's her reason. Ruth says, “Spread the corner of your garment over me, for you are a kinsman-redeemer.” (Ruth 3:9) She doesn't hand Boaz a long speech. She names who he is to her family.
The text never says Boaz owns the threshing floor, so it can't be Ruth's reason. What she says is, “…for you are a kinsman-redeemer.” (Ruth 3:9) The reason has to do with family, not property.

explanations.answer: He is a man of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Boaz does speak of the LORD right after this, when he says, “May the LORD bless you, my daughter.” (Ruth 3:10) But that's his line, not her reason. Ruth's reason is, “…for you are a kinsman-redeemer.” (Ruth 3:9)
True. Boaz says, “You have shown more kindness now than before…” (Ruth 3:10) Notice he says MORE kindness than before. He remembers what came earlier, and he's saying this tonight tops it.

It's actually True. Boaz says, “You have shown more kindness now than before, because you have not run after the younger men, whether rich or poor.” (Ruth 3:10) He isn't scolding her. He's telling her how well she has done.
Yes, character. Boaz says, “…all my fellow townspeople know that you are a woman of noble character.” (Ruth 3:11) That's what the whole town knows about her. Good character gets around, friend.

The word Boaz uses isn't birth. He says, “…all my fellow townspeople know that you are a woman of noble character.” (Ruth 3:11) Ruth is from Moab (Ruth 1:22), and that verse doesn't dig into where she was born. What he praises is who she is.
Wealth isn't what Boaz praises here. He says, “…you are a woman of noble character.” (Ruth 3:11) It's about the kind of person she is, not what's in her pockets. The word he uses is character.

This one is False, and there's the BUT. Boaz says, “Yes, it is true that I am a kinsman-redeemer, but there is a redeemer nearer than I.” (Ruth 3:12) So somebody else is closer. Boaz is honest about it right away.
Right, False. Boaz says, “Yes, it is true that I am a kinsman-redeemer, but there is a redeemer nearer than I.” (Ruth 3:12) He doesn't hide that from her. Somebody else is nearer than he is.
That's his promise. Boaz says, “But if he does not want to redeem you, as surely as the LORD lives, I will.” (Ruth 3:13) He ties his word to the LORD's name. That's a serious promise.

explanations.answer: He will send her back to Moab
explanations.explanation: Nothing about Moab in his answer. Boaz says, “But if he does not want to redeem you, as surely as the LORD lives, I will.” (Ruth 3:13) He says he will do it himself. Sending her anywhere isn't part of it.
Boaz doesn't go hunting for a third guy. He says, “…as surely as the LORD lives, I will.” (Ruth 3:13) The one stepping up is Boaz himself. No more names on the list.

This one is False. Boaz says, “Do not let it be known that a woman came to the threshing floor.” (Ruth 3:14) That's the opposite of spreading the word. And Ruth had already gotten up before anyone else could recognize her.

Right, False. Boaz says, “Do not let it be known that a woman came to the threshing floor.” (Ruth 3:14) He wants it kept quiet. Meanwhile I can't keep a batch of cookies quiet for ten minutes, because the smell tells on me.

Yes, barley. The text says, “…he poured in six measures of barley and placed it on her.” (Ruth 3:15) Barley is also what Boaz was winnowing on the threshing floor. The text even gives the count: six measures.

Wheat is part of Ruth's story, since she gleaned through the barley and wheat harvests (Ruth 2:23). But the grain Boaz pours into her shawl is barley. (Ruth 3:15) Right harvest, different grain for this verse.
Millet never shows up in this passage. What Boaz pours is “…six measures of barley…” (Ruth 3:15) The same grain he was winnowing that night. No millet, friend.

explanations.answer: Do not go back to your mother-in-law empty-handed
explanations.explanation: That's it. Ruth tells Naomi, “He gave me these six measures of barley, for he said, ‘Do not go back to your mother-in-law empty-handed.’…” (Ruth 3:17) Boaz is thinking of Naomi too. I think Ruth walked home with a full shawl and a full heart.

explanations.answer: Come back and glean in my field again tomorrow
explanations.explanation: Ruth did glean in Boaz's field (Ruth 2:23), so I see why this fits. But it isn't what Ruth says he told her here. She quotes him, “Do not go back to your mother-in-law empty-handed.” (Ruth 3:17)

explanations.answer: Share this grain with the servant girls tomorrow
explanations.explanation: The servant girls are in the story, but not in this line. Ruth reports that Boaz said, “Do not go back to your mother-in-law empty-handed.” (Ruth 3:17) The grain is for Ruth to bring home to Naomi.

explanations.answer: Boaz will not rest until it is settled today
explanations.explanation: Yes. Naomi says, “Wait, my daughter, until you find out how things go, for he will not rest unless he has resolved the matter today.” (Ruth 3:18) Naomi expects Boaz to settle it today. So she tells Ruth to wait.

explanations.answer: The nearer redeemer is away from town
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say where the nearer redeemer is. Naomi's reason is about Boaz: “…he will not rest unless he has resolved the matter today.” (Ruth 3:18) Nobody gets a travel schedule here.

explanations.answer: Boaz needs some time to think it over
explanations.explanation: Naomi gives a different reason. She says, “…he will not rest unless he has resolved the matter today.” (Ruth 3:18) Her focus is on Boaz resolving the matter that day.
